reading.title: When a successful pilot becomes an uncomfortable decision
reading.passage:
At the end of a six-month trial, the town's shared workspace appeared to have achieved precisely what its supporters had promised. Membership exceeded the original target, the building was occupied on most weekdays, and local newspapers had begun describing it as evidence that the high street could recover without another large retailer. The council was therefore surprised when the project manager recommended postponing expansion.

The recommendation was not a rejection of the workspace. It was an objection to the way its success was being represented. Membership figures counted people who had registered for a free introductory month, including those who had never returned. Occupancy figures combined paid desks with meeting rooms temporarily offered to community groups. Neither practice was necessarily misleading in isolation, but the two measures answered different questions. Together, they encouraged the impression that an established commercial service had already emerged.

The distinction mattered because the proposed extension would be financed on the assumption that subscription income could cover its running costs. The original building had benefited from reduced rent, volunteer reception staff and a repair budget paid by a separate regeneration grant. Those contributions were not expected to continue indefinitely. Replicating the visible features of the pilot without replicating its support would produce a different experiment, however familiar the floor plan looked.

Several council members objected that the manager's caution risked losing momentum. Small businesses had asked for more meeting rooms; a training provider wanted evening access; and a nearby landlord had offered a favourable lease that would expire within a month. Waiting for perfect evidence, they argued, could become an excuse for doing nothing. The manager accepted the criticism in principle but rejected its application. She had not asked for certainty. She had asked for a decision whose scale matched the uncertainty.

Her alternative was to rent part of the additional building for one year, with a break clause after six months. The extra space would be used initially for activities for which organisations had already expressed a willingness to pay. A modest evaluation budget would distinguish repeat paid use from initial curiosity and record which costs were being subsidised. Expansion into individual desks would depend on that evidence rather than on registrations alone.

This proposal had its own weaknesses. A short lease might make substantial improvements uneconomic, while organisations willing to pay for a room were not necessarily representative of independent workers seeking a daily desk. The manager acknowledged both points. Indeed, she insisted that they be included in the public report. Her purpose was not to substitute a flawless plan for a flawed one, but to make the unresolved assumptions visible enough to influence the next decision.

The council ultimately approved the limited lease. Its announcement nevertheless referred to an expansion 'following the success of the pilot'. That description was politically convenient and not entirely false. What it left out was the project's most useful achievement: it had taught the council to distinguish a promising service from a proven business model. Whether that lesson would survive the next round of publicity remained an open question.

questions.question_en: Why does the manager recommend postponing the original expansion despite favourable publicity?
questions.question_he: השיבו באנגלית והסבירו את הנימוק המרכזי.
questions.answer_en: The measures combine different kinds of participation and omit continuing subsidies, so they do not establish the commercial model on which the proposed expansion depends.

questions.question_en: Explain how two individually defensible measures produce a questionable combined impression.
questions.question_he: הסתמכו על שתי דוגמאות מן הטקסט.
questions.answer_en: Free registrations suggest demand, while occupancy includes free community use; together they imply established paid demand although neither measures repeat paid subscriptions.

questions.question_en: What assumption is challenged by the phrase 'however familiar the floor plan looked'?
questions.answer_en: Copying the physical arrangement does not reproduce the funding, volunteer support or operating conditions that helped the pilot succeed.

questions.question_en: How does the manager distinguish her position from waiting for perfect evidence?
questions.answer_en: She supports a smaller, reversible commitment tied to existing willingness to pay and better measurement, rather than demanding certainty before any action.

questions.question_en: Identify a limitation of the limited lease that the manager herself accepts.
questions.answer_en: Short tenure can make improvements uneconomic, or room-hiring organisations may not represent individual desk users, limiting what the next trial can establish.

questions.question_en: Is the final announcement simply a lie? Explain the writer's more qualified criticism.
questions.question_he: הציגו את המורכבות, בלי להסתפק בכן או לא.
questions.answer_en: It is partly justified because the service is promising, but its convenient framing obscures uncertainty about a sustainable business model and may erase the lesson about evidence.

listening.title: A project lead revises a recommendation
listening.passage:
Before we move to the vote, I want to clarify what I am recommending, because the summary circulated yesterday gives a rather firmer impression than I intended. I still support introducing the shared booking system. What I no longer support is introducing every part of it across all four offices on the same Monday.

The technical team has completed the tests we originally requested. The problem is that those tests establish whether the system behaves as specified, not whether our specification reflects the work people actually do. During the trial, reception staff described several arrangements that had never appeared in the written process: provisional bookings held while someone checks a customer's access needs, for example, and room changes agreed verbally when an appointment overruns. These are not necessarily bad habits. Some compensate for gaps in the formal process.

It would be tempting to treat the discovery as an argument for further training. There is certainly a training requirement, but telling people to follow a process does not resolve a case the process does not cover. If we launch the system unchanged, staff may create informal workarounds. We would then have cleaner records of the official workflow and less visibility of the actual one. That is the opposite of the improvement we are trying to make.

I am proposing a narrower first stage. Two offices would use the new system for straightforward bookings for six weeks. More complex appointments would remain on the current system, with an explicit record of why they were handled there. The other two offices would continue as they are for the same period. We would compare missed appointments, duplicate work and time spent resolving changes, rather than relying mainly on the number of bookings entered. A high number of entries would show adoption, but it would not by itself show that the work had become easier.

There are costs to this approach. Running two systems creates additional administration, and the offices selected for the first stage are already the most confident about the change. That makes the comparison imperfect. We can reduce the first problem by limiting the trial period, and we should report the second as a limitation rather than quietly presenting the results as representative of all four offices. I would also like one member of staff who has raised concerns to join the weekly review. Agreement within the trial team is not the same as evidence that the concerns have been answered.

Finally, the supplier's discounted implementation support expires at the end of this month. That gives us a genuine reason to decide promptly; it does not tell us which decision is right. We should compare the price of extending that support with the likely cost of a rushed rollout. My request today is to approve the limited first stage and authorise that comparison. It is not a request to cancel the project, and it should not be announced as approval of the full rollout. If the six-week results are encouraging, we will still need a separate decision about the more complicated appointments.

questions.question_en: What does the speaker still support, and what part of the original plan has changed?
questions.answer_en: She supports the shared booking system but opposes introducing all its features in all four offices at once.

questions.question_en: Why is additional training alone an inadequate response to the reception staff's examples?
questions.answer_en: Some real situations are absent from the specified workflow, so following it more carefully cannot resolve those missing cases.

questions.question_en: What paradox might result from launching the unchanged system?
questions.question_he: תארו את ההשפעה על התיעוד ועל העבודה בפועל.
questions.answer_en: Official records could become cleaner while informal workarounds make actual work less visible.

questions.question_en: Which outcomes would the first-stage evaluation prioritise over booking-entry counts?
questions.answer_en: Missed appointments, duplicate work and time spent resolving changes, rather than adoption alone.

questions.question_en: Why should a staff member who has raised concerns join the review?
questions.question_he: הסבירו את ההיגיון, לא רק את ההצעה.
questions.answer_en: To test whether concerns have been addressed instead of mistaking agreement among enthusiastic trial participants for evidence.

questions.question_en: How should the expiring discount influence the decision, according to the speaker?
questions.question_he: הבחינו בין דחיפות לבין הצדקה לתוכנית מסוימת.
questions.answer_en: It justifies a timely comparison of extending support with the cost of a rushed launch, but does not itself justify full rollout.

speaking.prompt_he: הקליטו באנגלית, עד 90 שניות: אתם מרכזים צוות שאמור לסיים פרויקט בעוד שבוע. מחלקה אחת מבקשת לדחות בשבועיים כדי לתקן בעיות איכות; מחלקה אחרת כבר התחייבה ללקוח. הציגו עמדה מאוזנת, הציעו פשרה מעשית, הסבירו סיכון שנשאר והתייחסו לטענה שהפשרה פוגעת באמון. אל תקראו טקסט שהכנתם מראש.
speaking.rubric_he: C1 diagnostic: a clear nuanced message; all four requested communicative functions; connected intelligible spontaneous discourse; flexible accurate language with appropriate qualification. Require at least 80 English words for sufficient range; transcript does not establish pronunciation. A rehearsed or typed response is not independent speaking evidence.

speaking.prompt_he: המשך בלתי צפוי: הלקוח מסכים לפשרה, אך דורש התחייבות לתאריך שאין לכם אפשרות להבטיח. הקליטו תשובה מקצועית באנגלית: הכירו בצורך שלו, הסבירו את גבול ההתחייבות, הציעו חלופה שניתן לבדוק ושאלו שאלה שמקדמת משא ומתן.
speaking.rubric_he: C1 diagnostic: acknowledgement and constructive negotiation; clear limit without unsupported promises; a verifiable alternative and useful question; appropriate register and flexible coherent language. Require a substantive response, at least 50 English words.

writing.prompt_he: כתבו באנגלית 250–400 מילים למנהלת ארגון: 68 מתוך 100 משתתפי קורס בחרו להשיב לסקר; 54 מהמשיבים דיווחו שהקורס מועיל. 42 מכלל המשתתפים השלימו מטלת ביצוע לפני ואחרי הקורס; 29 מהם השתפרו. אין קבוצת השוואה ולא ידוע מדוע אחרים לא נבדקו. ההנהלה שוקלת להכפיל את התקציב. נתחו מה הנתונים כן ולא תומכים בו, הסבירו שתי מגבלות, הציעו החלטה מידתית ותוכנית בדיקה. אל תמציאו נתונים, קשר סיבתי או מקורות.
writing.rubric_he: C1 diagnostic, written response only: accurate qualified interpretation distinguishing respondents from all participants and change from causation; complete recommendation plus two limitations and an evaluation plan; coherent well-signposted organization; flexible precise language and professional register. Require 250–400 English words. All four criteria are substantive. Do not reward invented statistics or causal certainty.
